name: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
title: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
answer: Weekly updates that make a difference are short, specific, frequent messages to families about missed assignments, grades, and absences, sent while there is still time to help. They matter because trials in middle and high schools and in low income schools in Chile found fewer course failures, better attendance, and higher math scores. AI can help teachers draft and personalize these updates, but the teacher reviews them before they go out.

sections.body: Many families only learn how a child is doing when a report card arrives, which can be too late to change the outcome. This idea solves that delay by sending parents short, concrete, frequent updates about missed assignments, grades, and absences. The updates are designed to give families information they can act on while there is still time. The book stresses that the evidence is for specific alerts, not for any message a school might send. General newsletters are useful, but they are not what the trials tested.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In middle and high schools, the tested approach sent weekly automated text messages to parents about missed assignments, grades, and absences. A trial in low income schools in Chile used weekly text messages about attendance, grades, and behavior. The messages were short, specific, and frequent, and they cost very little to send. AI can help a teacher draft short weekly summaries for a class, which are then personalized with each student's missing work and grades from the gradebook. Tools such as TalkingPoints can send the messages in families' languages, and the teacher reviews the messages before they go out.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports a randomized trial in middle and high schools in which weekly automated text messages to parents about missed assignments, grades, and absences cut course failures by 27 percent and raised class attendance by 12 percent (Bergman et al., 2021). A trial in low income schools in Chile found that weekly text messages to parents about attendance, grades, and behavior raised math scores by 0.09 standard deviations (Berlinski et al., 2021). The messages cost very little to send and worked by giving parents information they could act on. The evidence is for specific kinds of alerts, not for any message a school might send. General newsletters are useful but are not what the trials tested.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The evidence does not cover every message a school might send, so weekly updates should be built around concrete information such as a missed assignment or a low grade. They need to reach families while there is still time to act. General newsletters can be useful, but the trials did not test them, so they should not be presented as the same thing. AI can help draft and personalize updates, but the teacher reviews the messages before they go out. Schools keep the decisions about what specific information to include and how to design the updates.
